Hongkong - June 10th '49
Dear Family:
I left San Francisco May 24th on one of PAA's new Boeing Streto-
cruisers which carries 61 passengers on the upper deck and has space for 17.
more in a lower deck lounge reached by a eireuler staircase. The plane 1s
pressurized right from sea-level so there is no effect on your eers at all.
Our crossing in ten hours compares with my first crossing 13 years ago of 20
hours or more.
Bondy met me in Honolulu and drove me to the Royal Hawelian where &
room had been reserved for me.
The guests all looked 11ke black market op-
erators and I guess to stay there they have to be. I asked for a special rate
and got it - otherwise would have paid 130 per day.
The second day I "phoned
Debby Blekewell over on Kaual and asked her to have lunch with me at the most
attractive Kausi Inn near Lahul.
She wes so exeited that she nearly dropped
the iphone and I had to repeat everything I said to be sure she got it all
straight.
Kaual is only an hour by sir from Honolulu but the airport is at
one end of the Island and Debby and Pompy at the other end some 40 minutes
drive by car. Debby met me in her British Ford - Pompy joined us for Lunch
and we had lots of walla welle, sew the kids - very cute - the new house on
the beach which is just perfect, and then they drove me back to the airport.
Left Honolulu the next afternoon in a DC-l, Bleeperette and flew direct
to fake arriving there in the middle of the night so couldn't work the beach
for sea shells as I had on my previous trip. On to Tokyo arriving there May
30 early in the afternoon.
He laid over there until 2:30 a.m. when we de-
parted for Okinava - e refueling stop while Shanghei is closed .
We arrived
there esrly in the morning and atayed on the ground about an hour and one-half.
The harbors are dotted with the wrecks of ships many of which were American
boats caught there in a typhoon after V-J Day.
There was a long stretch of besch
nesr the airport but the PAA manager seid no shells.
The latter are on the
Pacific side some ten milea awey where the boya go swimming. He is going to
get some for me including "cats' eyes" which normally are found only in New
Zealand.
We arrived Hongkong after a flight along the east coast of Formosa.
The mountains of that island
rise up 1400 feet and while our direct flight
from Okinews to Hongkong would take us directly across Formosa we don't fly
that high in the DC-4's so - as previously stated - flew'along a nost for
biddire coast. The mountains come right down to the beach or terminate in
abrupt cliffs against which break the long rollers of the Pacifie. In more
than 30 miles of coast line I saw no sign of habitation either on the coast
or beek in the mountains - where dwell, I am told, an unconquered aborigine
mountain people who have held those mountain fastneases against Chinese and
Japanese alike.
Toward the southern tip of Formosa the mountains trail off
into a long flat point where there are small villages and farms. We flew over

that mountainless end of the island and on to Hongkong where we landed early
in the afternoon.
We were met by E. M. Allison, Ki Chun and Colonel C. I.
Liu and Jerry O'Donnell, PAA #1. The latter had secured a double room for
us in the Gloucester Hotel - one room being equipped with an air-conditioning
machine - very welcome 'cause Hongkong is about 90 in both temperature and
humidity.
That night we had Chinese chow - Szechuan style - with Max Polin.
I had forgot just how good it was !
The next day - Tuesday May 31 - we flew over to Canton with Colonel
It
wes & perfectly useless trip because he is of no importance and doesn't know
required by protocol. Arriving early at the airport me learned that the night
before the whole eabinet of Ho Ying-Chin had resigned - so our visit was
even less important. However, we went through with it and were rewarded by
a nice luncheon party in a bamboo grove on the outskirts of Canton not far
from the large rambling old residence which serves as the temporary head-
quarters for the Ministry. They are getting ready to move all the smell-fry
clerks to Chungking while the big shots will go to Formosa.
By a coincidence
only, of course, all the monetary funds - some 250 million US dollars - are
on Formoss! The new premier - old General Yen Shi-shan - is still forming
his cabinet and may or may not reappoint our present Minister of Conmunications.
The latter - 1ike all other Chinese officials - would rather not serve.
They d
all rather be free to make deels with the "liberation" authorities. Old Gen-
eral Yen is the same war lord who ran Shensi Province from 1911 until the Com-
munists captured his capital of Tai Yuan-fu some months ago. When the Japs
threatened Tai Yuan-fu he drove all around the city with a big sign which
announced that he would be is stinking furtle" - about as complimentary as
calling a Frenchman a pig - if he surrendered to the Japanese. The next day
he left with 20 truckloads of personel effects. He did put up & great battle
against the Communists and announced that he would die with his troops - but
he didn't. After lunch we drove into Shameen to see Lewis Clark, American
Minister. Did some shopping but found nothing. Canton is just the ssme ex-
cept that most of the rickshas are "bike" powered - which makes the traffic
worse.
Returning to Hongkong. It also re ains about the same - outwardly.
However, all is changed.
The old taipans are gone.
The Chinese have taken
They have invaded the Peak where formerly none but the first families
of British were permitted to live.
They have taken over the best hotels.
The Hongkong Hotel at "elevens" is 90% Chinese.
Stayed in Hongkong until Thursday then flew over to Manila to see
the new American Ambassador Mr. Marvin Cowan, nee Cohen. Spent Friday in
Manile.
You would never recognize the place.
Both wings of the magnificent
Government building - where the legislature sat - were shot to pieces and
have been torn down.
The old intramures is a mass of ruins with only an arch
or two remaining of the magnificent old churches. MacArthur's old headquarters
in the corner of the wall are not only gone but the wall too is no more.
stayed at the Manila Hotel which has been largely restored except that the fur-
niture is "retty" and the whole place has a "dow-et-the-heels" atmosphere.
Friday night I went out on to the dance floor about 11:30 to find only one
American (in shirt sleeves) and perhaps 100 Filipinos.

- 3 -
The Escolta is a row of dirty wooden shacks for the most part with
thousands upon thousands of Filipinos milling around in a maze of jeeps,
carametas, trucks, motor cars and taxis.
The din, dirt and confusion is
beyond description. In short, the far East has changed and will never again
return to the life out here as we once knew it.
Returning to Hongkong Saturday morning, there was no PAA schedule
for several days so I came over with Philippine Airways in a very fine DC-4.
Three other airplanes left that same morning all DC-3 type ships (not so good
for crossing so many miles of ocean) for China and I remembered that 16 years
ago we made the first round trip from Chine to the Philippines!
Returning here I found a cable relayed from New York to phone Geerge
Sellett.
The 'phone compeny said they would put me on the weiting list and
perhaps within four or five days I might get through.
However, All1 knew the
President and asked him for help. In a half hour I had George on the phone
He had planned to ask me to come out from New York
and was of course very pleased to know that I was already here. I called
again the next day and got a much better connection.
He said the "liberation"
euthorities were anxious to see us and were very glad that we were here.
thought that we would be permitted to resume Pan American service within e
few days or maybe a week.
That was the 5th of June and todey on the 10th me
have received no further word.
He hed lunch with Lewis Clerk yesterday and he advised us very
strongly to go over to Macao - intimating that Macao might become a very im-
portat point. You can draw your own conclusions! Bondy and I plan to go
over there Sunday the 12th and spend a few days. Will probably try to get
the Government to complete an air strip which is already partially con-
structed.
Will call on Gellion and our other friends over there.
Of course
if a green light is received from Shanghai will come right back.
My views regarding the whole Chinese situation have changed since
arriving here and talking to American, British and Chinese officials. I had
hoped that it might be possible for the Nationelists to get together and hold
a "beach-head" somewhere in South China. Of course anything can happen as
evidenced by the man who now sits in the White House.
But the situation
appears absolutely hopeless. Chiang Kai-shek will not let go. He is still
playing one political leader against another so that none will emerge to
challenge his position.
General Li - the acting President and General Pai
were the former strong men of Kwaagsi, the model Province.
The Generslissimo
is afraid that they may again gain complete control of Kwangsi and break away
from the so-celled "Central Government", so he has ordered General Pal to make
a stend with his Kwangsi troops au leng
Yang south of Changsha on the Hankow-
Canton Railroad. Chiang hopes - so they say - that General Pai and his troops
will be taken by the Communists and thus unable to retrest to Kwangsi. At
least that is the opinion of some usually well-informed
people. You remember
the old proverb - "Brothers stop quarrelling when there's a tiger at the door."
Well, the Nationalists are not following that idea and the concensus of
opinion is that the Communists will take Canton just as soon as their troops
have time to walk that far.
There may be a few provinces which will hold out
for months or maybe years against the Communists but they are in the west and
northwest beyond the reach of reil or river traffie and of little importance
58

- 4-
So - as I said above -- my views and hopes have changed. It is
clear that for ell practicable purposes the Communists are going to control
all of China.
Our only hope is to win them over to our side dow through
the years ahead. I believe the British Governent and the U.S. too will
accord them some form of recognition and get along with them the best we
Let's hope that being Chinese their good sense will predominate and
that while they may be 100% Russian-type today that tomorrow they may con-
promise in the old Chinese way and take at least a middle of the road
course.
Bondy and I are very much on the spot because 80% of CNAC is owned
by the Nationalist Government and we, representing the minority interest,
have to go along with the majority unless our own Government instruets us
to do otherwise and agrees to stand the consequences. So far we have had
little help from any quarter and I guess we'll have to work it out together
the best we can with our shaped heads.
We may get instructions any day to move the whole fleet of 50
airplanes to Formosa or Hainan.
Ali we can do is try to hold on until the
so-called National Government folds up and then try the best we can to get
along with the new regime.
In the meantime attempt - to the extent that
we can - to preserve the assets of CNAC.
There's never a dull moment !
Bix

properties.sfomuseum:description: Typewritten letter from Harold M. Bixby to his family, dated June 10, [1949] in Hong Kong, marked “Confidential”; includes description of trip from San Francisco to Hong Kong via Honolulu, Tokyo, and Okinawa on Boeing [377] Stratocruiser and Douglas DC-4 Sleeperette; views of Formosa, descriptions of Hong Kong, Manila, Canton [Guangzhou]; meeting in Manila with Ambassador Marvin Cowan; his assessment of the situation in China regarding the Nationalists and Communists and Chiang Kai-shek; mentions E.M. [Ernest] Allison, Ki Chun, Colonel C.Y. Liu, Jerry O’Donnell, the minister of communications, Lewis Clark, Bondy [William L. Bond].
